Third, the LLM app ecosystem is growing rapidly, and early characterization helps other platform designers avoid the same pitfall. Our demonstrations are limited to benign proof-of-concepts (redirecting a hotel search) rather than data exfiltration or credential theft.

Client-Side Analysis

Our analysis of the service framework was limited to client-side code delivered to and executed in the user’s browser, which is standard practice in web security research. The three undocumented parameters of sendFollowUpMessage were identified by observing the parameter handling in the runtime service-framework implementation; we did not circumvent any access controls, authentication mechanisms, or server-side protections.

Appendix A OpenAI Legacy Connectors

Table 8enumerates the 32 OpenAI first-party connectors present in the catalog. Unlike the 856 third-party MCP connectors, these carry no created_at timestamp and ship no client-side widgets.

30 of the 32 are legacy SERVICE integrations, which are server-side connectors to productivity tools such as Gmail, GitHub, Slack, and Notion. They are distributed via the default OAI catalog. The remaining 2 (Deep Research, Quizzes) are FIRST_PARTY_ECOSYSTEM apps listed in the public Ecosystem Directory. 29 of the 32 require OAuth authentication; the two ecosystem apps require none. These connectors also expose 353 server-side actions in total but no client-rendered UI. Their security model differs fundamentally from third-party MCP connectors: they execute within OpenAI’s own infrastructure and do not expose an Apps-SDK bridge surface.

Appendix C AST Analyzer Methodology (Detailed)

This appendix provides the detailed methodology behind the AST-based static analysis summarized in §2.3. We built two tools on top of our App Store crawl. First, an extractor retrieves each app’s client-side bundle, including any inline modules and referenced scripts loaded at runtime. Second, an AST-based static analyzer parses each bundle and identifies calls to APIs exposed through globalThis.openai. For each sendFollowUpMessage call site, the analyzer records which parameters are passed (including the undocumented ones) and whether each parameter is a static string literal or is constructed dynamically.

Parser

We use the Babel AST parser (@babel/parser, version 7.24) with the plugin set covering ES2022 syntax and JSX, since widget bundles are typically shipped as bundled React plus modern ES modules.

Alias and Minification Handling

For minified bundles, we resolve aliases by following local variable binding: a top-level const o = globalThis.openai followed by o.sendFollowUpMessage(...) is correctly resolved to the canonical API. We do not handle dynamic property access (o[fnName]) or higher-order wrappers (e.g., applyApi(o, ’sendFollowUpMessage’, args)); bundles that rely exclusively on these patterns are reported as unresolved and flagged in the selection-bias discussion below. Destructured assignment of globalThis.openai members into local names is resolved by the same binding walk.

Static vs. Dynamic Prompt Classifier

A prompt argument is classified as static if and only if it is a single string literal (i.e., a bare "..." or ’...’ with no interpolation). Any other construction, a template literal, a string concatenation expression (a + b), a variable reference, a function-return expression, or a spread into an object literal, is classified as dynamically constructed. The same classification applies to systemPrompt and to the hint parameter when present.

Appendix D Isolation Comparison (Detailed)

This appendix expands Table 4 in §5.4 with a per-platform walkthrough of isolation mechanisms.

Android/Linux: Namespaces and UIDs

Every Android app runs in its own Linux process with a unique UID and its own set of namespaces (PID, mount, network, user). Inter-process communication is impossible by default. When apps need to cooperate, they do so via explicit, kernel-mediated channels (Intents, Content Providers, Bound Services), each of which carries permission checks. The kernel knows which UID sent each message and can make access-control decisions accordingly.

iOS/macOS: Sandbox Profiles

Every iOS app is confined by the XNU kernel’s App Sandbox. A sandbox profile specifies which file paths, network endpoints, IPC channels, and system services the app may access. Apps that need to share data use App Groups, URL schemes, or App Extensions, all gated by entitlements that the system verifies. As on Android, the kernel has an unambiguous sense of “who is asking” and can enforce policies against each request.

Windows/macOS Desktop: Process Isolation

Desktop operating systems provide per-process address spaces for memory protection, together with kernel-mediated inter-process communication via pipes, sockets, and shared memory whose access is gated by ACLs on the underlying kernel objects. These are two separable mechanisms (memory protection is not the same as IPC access control), not a single “process isolation” primitive. Each process has a distinct memory space, distinct file handles, and distinct credentials, and the kernel mediates every cross-process boundary crossing.

callTool Scoping

The confused-deputy framing in §5.1 rests on the claim that only the LLM, not individual apps, can dispatch tool calls across connectors. We argue callTool is app-local based on two observations. First, the service framework’s deobfuscated dispatch logic resolves the tool identifier against the calling connector’s registered tool set before forwarding to the host; a tool name not present in that set does not reach the host. Second, in attempted cross-connector callTool invocations (app A naming app B’s tool by the exact identifier app B registers) the host returned a dispatch error in every case; no invocation reached app B. If either observation were falsified in future platform updates, the confused-deputy framing would reduce to direct ambient-authority abuse, which would strengthen the severity of the finding rather than weaken it.
